s0003.literal: Zhou Tiehu; Cheng Lingxi; son Wenji
s0003.idiomatic: Zhou Tiehu; Cheng Lingxi; son Wenji

s0004.literal: Zhou Tiehu—no one knew where he was from; in the Liang era he crossed south.
s0004.idiomatic: Zhou Tiehu came from no known place. Under Liang he crossed south with the migration.

s0005.literal: His speech was thick with a northern accent; his physical strength surpassed other men; he was skilled with horse and spear; he served Liang's Prince of Hedong, Xiao Yu, and was known for courage; Yu appointed him by commission as military adjutant in the prince's establishment.
s0005.idiomatic: He spoke with a heavy northern accent, had uncommon strength, and fought well from horseback with the spear. He served Liang's Prince of Hedong, Xiao Yu, and won a name for bravery. Yu commissioned him military adjutant in the princely staff.

s0006.literal: When Yu became Inspector of Guangzhou, he made Tiehu magistrate of Xingning.
s0006.idiomatic: When Yu became inspector of Guangzhou, he made Tiehu magistrate of Xingning.

s0007.literal: When Yu was transferred to Xiangzhou, Tiehu was again made magistrate of Linzheng.
s0007.idiomatic: When Yu moved to Xiangzhou, Tiehu was again made magistrate of Linzheng.

s0008.literal: In Hou Jing's rebellion, Emperor Yuan at Jingzhou sent the heir Fangdeng to replace Yu and also advanced troops against him.
s0008.idiomatic: During Hou Jing's rebellion, Emperor Yuan of Liang at Jingzhou sent his heir Fangdeng to replace Yu and marched troops against him.

s0009.literal: Yu resisted in battle and won a great victory; Fangdeng died; Tiehu's merit was foremost; Yu entrusted and favored him heavily.
s0009.idiomatic: Yu fought back and won a crushing victory. Fangdeng was killed. Tiehu's merit stood first, and Yu relied on him ever more heavily.

s0010.literal: When Wang Sengbian campaigned against Yu, he captured Tiehu in the battle line; Sengbian ordered him boiled alive; Tiehu cried out: "Hou Jing is not yet destroyed—how can you kill a stalwart?
s0010.idiomatic: When Wang Sengbian attacked Yu, he took Tiehu on the field. Sengbian ordered him boiled alive. Tiehu shouted, "Hou Jing is not yet destroyed—why kill a fighting man?

s0011.literal: " Sengbian marveled at his words, then pardoned him and returned him to his command.
s0011.idiomatic: " Sengbian was struck by his words, spared him, and returned him to his troops.

s0012.literal: When Hou Jing marched west, Tiehu followed Sengbian in defeating Ren Yue, captured Song Zixian, and in every battle had merit.
s0012.idiomatic: When Hou Jing marched west, Tiehu followed Sengbian against Ren Yue, took Song Zixian prisoner, and earned merit in every fight.

s0013.literal: Under Emperor Yuan's provisional mandate he was made General of Benevolent Prestige and Inspector of Tongzhou, enfeoffed as Viscount of Dunyang county with a fief of three hundred households.
s0013.idiomatic: Under Emperor Yuan's provisional commission he was made general of benevolent prestige and inspector of Tongzhou, and enfeoffed as Viscount of Dunyang with three hundred households.

s0014.literal: He again followed Sengbian in recovering the capital, received the surrender of Xie Daren, and pacified Lu Na in Xiangzhou.
s0014.idiomatic: He again followed Sengbian in recovering the capital, took Xie Daren's surrender, and pacified Lu Na in Xiangzhou.

s0015.literal: In the second year of Chengsheng, for his successive battle merits he was advanced to marquis, his fief increased together with the previous to five hundred households.
s0015.idiomatic: In the second year of Chengsheng (552), for repeated battle honors he was raised to marquis, his fief brought to five hundred households in all.

s0016.literal: He was then made Scattered Cavalry Regular Attendant, concurrently Administrator of Xinyi, general as before.
s0016.idiomatic: He was then made scattered-cavalry regular attendant and concurrently administrator of Xinyi, retaining his general's rank.

s0017.literal: The Founder executed Sengbian; Tiehu led his command in surrender and thereby recovered his former post.
s0017.idiomatic: When the Founder killed Sengbian, Tiehu surrendered with his command and was restored to his former post.

s0018.literal: Xu Sihui brought Qi invaders across the river; at Banqiao Ford Tiehu broke their river army and captured all their armor, weapons, and boats.
s0018.idiomatic: Xu Sihui brought Qi troops across the Yangzi. At Banqiao Ford Tiehu shattered their fleet and seized their armor, weapons, and vessels entire.

s0019.literal: He also attacked Liyang, raided the Qi invaders' infantry camps, and in every case won success.
s0019.idiomatic: He attacked Liyang, struck the Qi army's foot camps, and won every engagement.

s0020.literal: When Sihui was pacified, in the second year of Shaotai he was transferred to Scattered Cavalry Regular Attendant, Stern Prestige General, and Left Defender of the Heir Apparent.
s0020.idiomatic: After Sihui was suppressed, in the second year of Shaotai (555) he was made scattered-cavalry regular attendant, stern-prestige general, and left defender of the heir.

s0021.literal: Soon he followed Zhou Wenyü on the Southern River to resist Xiao Bo, always serving as vanguard.
s0021.idiomatic: Soon he followed Zhou Wenyü on the Southern River against Xiao Bo and always led the van.

s0022.literal: Wenyü also ordered Tiehu with a detached force to strike Bo's vanguard Ouyang Hui at Kuchu Ford.
s0022.idiomatic: Wenyü also sent Tiehu with a detached column to hit Bo's vanguard Ouyang Hui at Kuchu Ford.

s0023.literal: He again followed Wenyü west against Wang Lin; at Dankou they were defeated; Tiehu, with Wenyü and Hou Andu, were all taken by Lin.
s0023.idiomatic: He marched west again with Wenyü against Wang Lin. At Dankou the army was broken, and Tiehu, Wenyü, and Hou Andu were all captured.

s0024.literal: Lin summoned the generals to audience and spoke with them; only Tiehu's words and bearing were unyielding; therefore Lin pardoned all Wenyü's party but Tiehu alone was killed; he was forty-nine.
s0024.idiomatic: Lin called the generals before him. Only Tiehu answered without bending. Lin spared Wenyü and the rest but put Tiehu to death. He was forty-nine.

s0025.literal: When the Founder heard of it, he issued an edict saying: "The treasure of Heaven and Earth is life itself; among embodied souls nothing is heavier than fate.
s0025.idiomatic: When the Founder heard, he issued an edict: "Heaven and earth treasure life above all; among mortal men nothing weighs like a single fate.

s0026.literal: As for giving life to establish integrity and laying down life to repay kindness—when one looks back on the distant past and cherishes the former age, honor should indeed be raised by degrees.
s0026.idiomatic: To throw away life for principle and spend one's last breath repaying grace—when the court looks back on such men, honor must rise by degrees.

s0027.literal: Scattered Cavalry Regular Attendant, Stern Prestige General, Left Defender of the Heir Apparent, Inspector of Tongzhou, Administrator of Xinyi, and Marquis of Dunyang county Tiehu—his bearing was deep and weighty, his martial spirit brave and strong; north and south he campaigned, exhausting loyalty and strength.
s0027.idiomatic: Scattered-cavalry regular attendant, stern-prestige general, left defender of the heir, inspector of Tongzhou, administrator of Xinyi, and Marquis of Dunyang, Tiehu—deep of bearing, fierce in the field—fought north and south until loyalty and strength were spent.

s0028.literal: He drove the van at Jiangxia and fell among the rebels; his spirit grew only sterner; he spoke freely and would not bend.
s0028.idiomatic: He led the charge at Jiangxia and fell into the rebels' hands. His spirit only hardened; he spoke plainly and would not yield.

s0029.literal: Was this not like Wen Xu meeting death and stroking his beard, or Pang De at the last hour still glaring with anger?
s0029.idiomatic: Was this not Wen Xu at his death, stroking his beard, or Pang De at the end still glaring in wrath?

s0030.literal: Loyalty and constancy such as this move pity to the depths; he may be posthumously made Palace Attendant, General Who Protects the Army, and Inspector of Qing and Ji provinces; his fief is increased by one thousand households; a suite of war drums is granted; his marquisate is unchanged.
s0030.idiomatic: Constancy such as this stirs the deepest grief. Let him be posthumously palace attendant, general who protects the army, and inspector of Qing and Ji; add one thousand households to his fief; grant a suite of war drums; let his marquisate stand as before.

s0031.literal: " In the fifth year of Tiancheng, Emperor Wen again issued an edict saying: "Han dynasty meritorious ministers had their forms painted in the palace halls; Wei dynasty fierce generals had their names joined to the ancestral temple—thus merit endures and generations do not forget.
s0031.idiomatic: " In the fifth year of Tiancheng (564), Emperor Wen again decreed: "Han worthies were painted in the palace; Wei champions were named in the ancestral shrine—so merit lives on and ages do not forget.

s0032.literal: The late Palace Attendant, General Who Protects the Army, Inspector of Qing and Ji provinces, and Marquis of Dunyang county Tiehu—his loyalty was upright and bright, his strength bold; when the royal enterprise was first founded he was caught in the course of events; wings folded in the rebel camp, he kept his color in the enemy's court—an ancient hero; the discerning share his awe.
s0032.idiomatic: The late palace attendant, general who protects the army, inspector of Qing and Ji, and Marquis of Dunyang, Tiehu—upright in loyalty, bold in battle—was caught when the dynasty was young, yet in the rebels' camp he kept his color before the foe, a hero of old days whom all who knew him admired.

s0033.literal: He fell without yielding; though glory was heaped on him, the returning soul is far; words of praise and regret follow.
s0033.idiomatic: He died unbowed. Though honors were piled on him, his spirit is far; the court speaks only praise and regret.

s0034.literal: He should attend the Founder's tomb mound and receive sacrificial offerings with reverence; he may share offerings in the Founder's temple hall.
s0034.idiomatic: Let him attend the Founder's mound and receive sacrifice with reverence, and share offerings in the Founder's temple.

s0036.literal: At that time there was Ma Ming of Xuyi, styled Shilang, who under Liang served the Prince of Poyang, Xiao Fan.
s0036.idiomatic: At that time Ma Ming of Xuyi, styled Shilang, had served under Liang the Prince of Poyang, Xiao Fan.

s0037.literal: In Hou Jing's rebellion he held the eastern border of Lujiang and resisted the rebels at the Lincheng stockade.
s0037.idiomatic: In Hou Jing's rebellion he held Lujiang's eastern border and held the rebels at bay at the Lincheng stockade.

s0038.literal: Emperor Yuan appointed him Scattered Cavalry Regular Attendant, General Who Pacifies the North, Inspector of Beixi province, and concurrently Administrator of Lujiang.
s0038.idiomatic: Emperor Yuan made him scattered-cavalry regular attendant, general who pacifies the north, inspector of Beixi, and concurrently administrator of Lujiang.

s0039.literal: When Jingzhou fell, he came over to the Founder.
s0039.idiomatic: When Jingzhou fell he submitted to the Founder.

s0040.literal: In the Shaotai era his offices were restored; he was enfeoffed Marquis of Xihua county with a fief of two thousand households.
s0040.idiomatic: In the Shaotai era his offices were restored and he was enfeoffed Marquis of Xihua with two thousand households.

s0041.literal: He too followed Wenyü west against Wang Lin; at Dankou the army was defeated; Ming fought fiercely and died; he was posthumously given the Staff of Authority, General Who Pacifies the West, and Inspector of Yingzhou.
s0041.idiomatic: He too followed Wenyü west against Wang Lin. At Dankou the army was broken; Ming fought to the death. He was posthumously given the staff of authority, made general who pacifies the west, and inspector of Yingzhou.

s0042.literal: Cheng Lingxi, styled Xuantidi, was a native of Haining in Xin'an.
s0042.idiomatic: Cheng Lingxi, styled Xuantidi, was a native of Haining in Xin'an.

s0043.literal: From youth he was known for courage and strength; on foot he could cover more than two hundred li in a day; he was skilled in riding and swimming.
s0043.idiomatic: From youth he was known for strength and daring. On foot he could cover more than two hundred li in a day; he rode and swam with ease.

s0044.literal: At the end of Liang, in Haining, Yi, She, and other counties and on the borders of Poyang and Xuancheng commanderies bandits were many; nearby counties suffered from them.
s0044.idiomatic: At the end of Liang, Haining, Yi, She, and the borderlands of Poyang and Xuancheng were thick with bandits, and neighboring counties suffered.

s0045.literal: Lingxi had long been feared in his home district; successive magistrates constantly had him recruit young men to pursue and capture robbers.
s0045.idiomatic: Lingxi had long been feared in his home country. Magistrates before and after him constantly had him raise young men to hunt down brigands.

s0046.literal: In Hou Jing's rebellion Lingxi gathered followers and held Yi and She to resist Jing.
s0046.idiomatic: In Hou Jing's rebellion Lingxi gathered followers and held Yi and She against Jing.

s0047.literal: Jing's army held Xin'an; the Administrator of Xin'an, Marquis of Xiangxi village, Xiao Yin, fled to rely on Lingxi; Lingxi received him as alliance chief.
s0047.idiomatic: Jing's army held Xin'an. The administrator, Marquis of Xiangxi village Xiao Yin, fled to Lingxi, who took him as head of the alliance.

s0048.literal: Emperor Yuan of Liang at Jingzhou assumed provisional authority; he also sent envoys by hidden routes to present memorials.
s0048.idiomatic: Emperor Yuan of Liang at Jingzhou took provisional authority; Lingxi also sent envoys by secret paths to present memorials.

s0049.literal: Liu Shenmao raised righteous arms at Dongyang to resist the rebels; Lingxi took Xin'an and coordinated with Shenmao.
s0049.idiomatic: Liu Shenmao raised arms at Dongyang against the rebels. Lingxi took Xin'an and acted in concert with him.

s0050.literal: Emperor Yuan appointed him Bearer of the Staff, Regular Attendant of Direct Communication, Commander-in-Chief of all military affairs in Xin'an commandery, Cloud-Banner General, Inspector of Qiao province with credentials, concurrently Administrator of Xin'an, and enfeoffed Marquis of Baqiu county with a fief of five hundred households.
s0050.idiomatic: Emperor Yuan gave him the staff, made him regular attendant of direct communication and commander of all forces in Xin'an, cloud-banner general and inspector of Qiao with credentials, administrator of Xin'an, and Marquis of Baqiu with five hundred households.

s0051.literal: Shenmao was broken by Jing; Jing's lieutenant Lü Zirong advanced against Xin'an; Lingxi withdrew to hold Yi and She.
s0051.idiomatic: Shenmao was defeated by Jing. Jing's lieutenant Lü Zirong pressed Xin'an; Lingxi fell back to Yi and She.

s0052.literal: When Jing was defeated, Zirong withdrew; Lingxi again held Xin'an.
s0052.idiomatic: When Jing fell, Zirong withdrew and Lingxi recovered Xin'an.

s0053.literal: He advanced on Jiande and captured the rebel chief Zhao Sanggan.
s0053.idiomatic: He advanced on Jiande and captured the rebel chief Zhao Sanggan.

s0054.literal: For his merit he was given the Staff, made Scattered Cavalry Regular Attendant, Commander-in-Chief of all military affairs in Qing and Ji provinces, and Inspector of Qing province; his fief was increased together with the previous to one thousand households; general and administrator as before.
s0054.idiomatic: For merit he received the staff, was made scattered-cavalry regular attendant, commander of Qing and Ji, and inspector of Qing; his fief rose to one thousand households in all; he kept his general's rank and the administration.

s0055.literal: He was then ordered to lead his command down to Yangzhou to assist Wang Sengbian in garrison defense.
s0055.idiomatic: He was then ordered to lead his command to Yangzhou to help Wang Sengbian hold the garrison.

s0056.literal: He was transferred to Administrator of Wuxing; before he took up the post Sengbian ordered Lingxi to follow Hou Tian west to relieve Jingzhou.
s0056.idiomatic: He was named administrator of Wuxing, but before he went Sengbian sent him with Hou Tian west to relieve Jingzhou.

s0057.literal: Jingzhou fell; he returned to the capital.
s0057.idiomatic: Jingzhou fell and he returned to the capital.

s0058.literal: The Founder executed Sengbian; Lingxi led his command to come to the rescue; his troops fought fiercely at Shitou's western gate; Editorial footnote marker 1. the army fared ill; envoys were sent to summon and instruct him; only after a long time did he surrender; the Founder deeply approved his conduct.
s0058.idiomatic: When the Founder killed Sengbian, Lingxi marched to his aid. His men fought hard at Shitou's western gate. [1] The battle went against them. Messengers were sent to summon and persuade him; only after long delay did he yield. The Founder held his conduct in high esteem.

s0059.literal: In the first year of Shaotai he was given the Staff of Authority, made Trustworthy Martial General and Administrator of Lanling, regular attendant as before, to assist in defending Jingkou.
s0059.idiomatic: In the first year of Shaotai (555) he received the staff, was made trustworthy-martial general and administrator of Lanling, retaining his attendant post, to help defend Jingkou.

s0060.literal: When Xu Sihui was pacified Lingxi had merit; he was made Administrator of South Danyang, enfeoffed Marquis of Suian county, his fief increased together with the previous to one thousand five hundred households; he still garrisoned Caishi.
s0060.idiomatic: When Xu Sihui was suppressed Lingxi earned merit. He was made administrator of South Danyang, enfeoffed Marquis of Suian, his fief brought to one thousand five hundred households in all, and continued to hold Caishi.

s0061.literal: He followed Zhou Wenyü west to attack Wang Lin; at Dankou they were defeated and he was detained by Lin.
s0061.idiomatic: He followed Zhou Wenyü west against Wang Lin. At Dankou the army was broken and Lin held him prisoner.

s0062.literal: The next year he escaped back with Hou Andu and others.
s0062.idiomatic: The next year he escaped back with Hou Andu and the rest.

s0063.literal: He was concurrently Administrator of Danyang; he went out as Administrator of Gaotang and Taiyuan commanderies and still garrisoned Nanling.
s0063.idiomatic: He was concurrently administrator of Danyang, then went out as administrator of Gaotang and Taiyuan and still held Nanling.

s0064.literal: He was transferred to Left Defender of the Heir Apparent.
s0064.idiomatic: He was transferred to left defender of the heir.

s0065.literal: When the Founder died, Wang Lin's vanguard marched east; Lingxi defeated it at Nanling, captured its soldiers, and also seized more than ten green-dragon coaches.
s0065.idiomatic: When the Founder died, Wang Lin's vanguard marched east. Lingxi broke it at Nanling, took its troops prisoner, and seized more than ten green-dragon coaches.

s0066.literal: For his merit he was given the Staff, made Commander-in-Chief of all military affairs along the Yangzi frontier in South Yuzhou, Trustworthy Martial General, and Inspector of South Yuzhou.
s0066.idiomatic: For merit he received the staff and was made commander of South Yuzhou's river frontier forces, trustworthy-martial general, and inspector of South Yuzhou.

s0067.literal: Hou Tian and others defeated Wang Lin at Zhakou; Lingxi pursued the victory north and held Lushan.
s0067.idiomatic: Hou Tian and others defeated Wang Lin at Zhakou. Lingxi pressed the rout and took Lushan.

s0068.literal: He was summoned to be Left Guard General; Editorial footnote marker 2. the rest as before.
s0068.idiomatic: He was recalled as left guard general; [2] all else unchanged.

s0069.literal: In the fourth year of Tiancheng, Zhou Di again raided Linchuan heavily; Lingxi was made commander-in-chief; from a separate route through Poyang he struck Di, and Di again fled into the mountain valleys.
s0069.idiomatic: In the fourth year of Tiancheng (563) Zhou Di raided Linchuan again. Lingxi was made commander and, marching from Poyang by a separate route, drove Di back into the hills.

s0070.literal: In the fifth year he was transferred to Central Protector of the Army, regular attendant as before.
s0070.idiomatic: In the fifth year he was made central protector of the army, retaining his attendant rank.

s0071.literal: He went out with the Staff of Authority as Commander-in-Chief of all military affairs in Ying, Ba, and Wu provinces, Manifest Resolution General, and Inspector of Ying province.
s0071.idiomatic: He went out with the staff as commander of Ying, Ba, and Wu, manifest-resolution general, and inspector of Ying.

s0072.literal: When the Deposed Emperor took the throne, his title was advanced to Cloud-Banner General.
s0072.idiomatic: When the Deposed Emperor came to the throne his title was raised to cloud-banner general.

s0073.literal: When Hua Jiao rebelled he sent envoys to win Lingxi over; Lingxi executed Jiao's envoys and reported the matter.
s0073.idiomatic: When Hua Jiao rebelled he sent envoys to win Lingxi over. Lingxi killed Jiao's messengers and reported it.

s0074.literal: The court deeply praised his loyalty, strengthened his defenses, granted a suite of war drums, and therefore treated him with open heart, having his son Wenji lead the river army to assist in defense.
s0074.idiomatic: The court praised his loyalty, reinforced his defenses, granted a suite of war drums, and treated him with full trust, putting his son Wenji in charge of the river force to help hold the post.

s0075.literal: At that time Zhou sent its general the Duke of Changhu, Tuoba Ding, with twenty thousand foot and horse to assist Jiao in besieging Lingxi; Lingxi closed the city and held firm.
s0075.idiomatic: Zhou then sent its general the Duke of Changhu, Tuoba Ding, with twenty thousand foot and horse to help Jiao besiege Lingxi. Lingxi shut the walls and held.

s0076.literal: When Jiao withdrew, he then led his army in pursuit of Ding; Ding could not cross the river and surrendered with his troops.
s0076.idiomatic: When Jiao withdrew, Lingxi marched out and pursued Ding. Ding could not cross the river and surrendered with his army.

s0077.literal: He then advanced against Zhou's Mian province, took it, and captured its inspector Pei Kuan.
s0077.idiomatic: He then attacked Zhou's Mian province, took it, and captured its inspector Pei Kuan.

s0078.literal: For his merit his title was advanced to Pacifying West General; he was re-enfeoffed Duke of Chong'an county; his fief was increased together with the previous to two thousand households.
s0078.idiomatic: For merit his title rose to pacifying-west general; he was re-enfeoffed Duke of Chong'an; his fief reached two thousand households in all.

s0079.literal: Lingxi's nature was stern and harsh; in commanding subordinates he was very severe; for small offenses among the soldiers he invariably executed them by military law; in idle moments he would add beatings; yet his orders were clear, he shared hardship and comfort with the soldiers, and the troops for that reason attached themselves to him.
s0079.idiomatic: Lingxi was harsh by nature and ruled his men with iron severity. Small faults brought military execution; idle moments brought the lash. Yet his orders were clear, he shared hardship with the ranks, and the troops clung to him for it.

s0080.literal: By nature he loved planting; he personally labored at tillage; as to what suited land and water, when to reap and harvest—though old farmers could not match him.
s0080.idiomatic: He loved to plant and worked the fields himself. What suited wet land or dry, when to cut and when to gather—veteran farmers could not match him.

s0081.literal: His concubines had no idle hands; all were pressed to spin and weave.
s0081.idiomatic: His concubines had no idle hands; all were set to spin and weave.

s0082.literal: As for distributing wealth in expenditure, he was not stingy.
s0082.idiomatic: When he spent, he did not count small coins.

s0083.literal: In the second year of Guangda he died in his province, aged fifty-five.
s0083.idiomatic: In the second year of Guangda (568) he died in office, aged fifty-five.

s0084.literal: He was posthumously made Pacifying West General and Grand Master with the Golden Seal and Purple Cord; posthumous name Zhongzhuang.
s0084.idiomatic: He was posthumously made pacifying-west general and grand master with the golden seal and purple cord, with the posthumous name Zhongzhuang.

s0085.literal: In the fourth year of Taijian an edict ordered him to share offerings in the Founder's temple hall.
s0085.idiomatic: In the fourth year of Taijian (572) an edict ordered him to share offerings in the Founder's temple.

s0088.literal: From childhood he practiced riding and archery; he had much resourcefulness; he was resolute and had his father's manner.
s0088.idiomatic: From boyhood he trained in riding and archery, had his father's resource, and was resolute in his father's mold.

s0089.literal: At twenty he followed Lingxi on campaigns and always was first to scale the ramparts and break the line.
s0089.idiomatic: At twenty he followed Lingxi on campaign and was always first over the wall and into the breach.

s0090.literal: When Lingxi, with Zhou Wenyü and Hou Andu, were defeated at Dankou and taken by Wang Lin, the Founder summoned the sons of generals who had fallen into the enemy and treated them generously; Wenji had the finest bearing and was deeply prized by the Founder.
s0090.idiomatic: When Lingxi, Wenyü, and Hou Andu were beaten at Dankou and held by Wang Lin, the Founder summoned the sons of captured generals and treated them well. Wenji bore himself best and won the Founder's deep regard.

s0091.literal: In the Yongding era he was repeatedly promoted to Regular Attendant of Direct Communication and magistrate of Jurong.
s0091.idiomatic: In the Yongding era he rose through regular attendant of direct communication to magistrate of Jurong.

s0092.literal: When Emperor Wen succeeded to the throne, he was made Central Straight Military Adjutant within the limits of the Manifest Favor Prince of Shixing's establishment.
s0092.idiomatic: When Emperor Wen succeeded, he was made central straight military adjutant in the establishment of the Manifest Favor Prince of Shixing.

s0093.literal: At that time the prince was Inspector of Yangzhou and garrisoned Yecheng; all military affairs of the establishment were entrusted to him.
s0093.idiomatic: The prince was then inspector of Yangzhou, holding Yecheng; all military business of the staff was placed in Wenji's hands.

s0094.literal: In the second year of Tiancheng he was made Steadfast Resolution General and Administrator of Xin'an, and still followed Hou Andu east against Liu Yi.
s0094.idiomatic: In the second year of Tiancheng (561) he was made steadfast-resolution general and administrator of Xin'an, and marched east with Hou Andu against Liu Yi.

s0095.literal: Yi's partisan Xiang Wenzheng held Xin'an; Wenji led three hundred picked armored men and went lightly to attack him.
s0095.idiomatic: Yi's man Xiang Wenzheng held Xin'an. Wenji took three hundred picked armored men and struck lightly.

s0096.literal: Wenzheng sent his elder brother's son Zan to resist; Wenji fought him, broke Zan's army completely, and Wenzheng then surrendered.
s0096.idiomatic: Wenzheng sent his brother's son Zan to meet him. Wenji routed Zan's force and Wenzheng surrendered.

s0097.literal: In the third year the Prince of Shixing, Boma, went out to garrison the eastern province; Wenji was again made military adjutant of the Eastern Garrison establishment, concurrently magistrate of Shan.
s0097.idiomatic: In the third year the Prince of Shixing, Boma, took up the eastern garrison; Wenji was again made military adjutant of the eastern staff, concurrently magistrate of Shan.

s0098.literal: In the fourth year Chen Baoying joined with Liu Yi; he also sent troops with Zhou Di to come out again at Linchuan; Emperor Wen sent the Administrator of Xinyi, Yu Xiaoxiang, by the sea route to strike Jin'an; Wenji served as his vanguard; wherever he went he won.
s0098.idiomatic: In the fourth year Chen Baoying allied with Liu Yi and sent troops with Zhou Di against Linchuan again. Emperor Wen sent Yu Xiaoxiang, administrator of Xinyi, by sea against Jin'an with Wenji as vanguard. Everywhere they went they prevailed.

s0099.literal: When Chen Baoying was pacified Wenji's battle merit was greatest; on return he was transferred to advisory military adjutant of the establishment, concurrently commanding the central straight guard.
s0099.idiomatic: When Baoying was suppressed Wenji's battle merit stood first. On return he was made advisory military adjutant of the staff, still commanding the central straight guard.

s0100.literal: He went out as Administrator of Linhai.
s0100.idiomatic: He went out as administrator of Linhai.
